name: IGF-1 LR3
summary: A lab-made, more potent form of IGF-1 that escapes the body's IGF-1 binding proteins, sold as a research chemical for muscle growth; evidence is limited to lab studies.
what_it_is: IGF-1 LR3 (Long R3 IGF-1) is an engineered version of insulin-like growth factor 1, the hormone that carries out some of growth hormone's effects, including on muscle. It has arginine in place of glutamic acid at position 3 plus a 13-amino-acid extension at the front end; these changes make it bind poorly to the IGF-binding proteins that normally hold IGF-1 in check, so it acts more strongly. Natural IGF-1 (mecasermin) is sold as a medicine for rare conditions such as primary IGF-1 deficiency, but the LR3 analog is not approved for human use.

evidence.why: Its extra potency comes from lab studies; no human studies were identified, and a review notes little evidence that IGF-1 improves performance in healthy people.

status_us.label: Not approved; not on FDA's compounding lists
status_us.note: IGF-1 LR3 is not an approved drug and does not appear on FDA's 503A or 503B lists of nominated bulk substances, so pharmacies have no recognized basis to compound it. WADA bans IGF-1 and its analogues in sport at all times.

benefits.claim: Stronger IGF-1 activity than natural IGF-1 in lab studies, because it binds poorly to IGF-binding proteins
Taken by athletes for muscle growth, but a review found little information on whether IGF-1 improves performance in healthy people

risks.risk: Effects in people are unknown: no human studies of the analog were identified, and data on IGF-1 in healthy people are scarce
Escapes the binding proteins that normally buffer IGF-1, which makes it more potent; the consequences in people are untested
Lab-only IGF-1 products have reached athletes and black-market supplements have contained IGF-1 analogs, so identity and purity are uncertain
Approved drugs that raise IGF-1, such as tesamorelin, carry label warnings about tumor growth in people with cancer

avoid_if: Competitive athletes (prohibited by WADA at all times)

before: General health check with a clinician
labs.why: No evidence-based monitoring exists for this research chemical, because it has not been studied in people.

studies.title: Growth Hormone Doping in Sports: A Critical Review of Use and Detection Strategies
studies.finding: Describes Long-R3-IGF-I as a more potent IGF-1 analog with low affinity for IGF-binding proteins, notes IGF-1 analogs have been found in black-market supplements, and finds little information on IGF-1's performance effects in healthy people.

ask_your_clinician: What lawful, studied options exist for my muscle or body-composition goal?
Given my cancer history and blood sugar, is any IGF-1 product safe for me?
If I compete in a tested sport, would this cause an anti-doping violation?

notes_for_editor: Very thin sourcing: the web-search budget ran out before the primary animal studies (e.g., Francis 1992; Tomas 1993 in rats) or the mecasermin (Increlex) label could be opened, so almost everything rests on the 2012 Endocrine Reviews article. Low blood sugar, the main labeled risk of mecasermin and the prototype's top risk (with an insulin/glucose-lowering-drug interaction), could not be confirmed from an opened source and is left out of risks and interactions; please add it from the Increlex label. The diabetes caution in avoid_if is kept as general prudence. 'No recognized basis to compound' is an inference from FDA's lists and 503A rules.
